datasource_item.source_question_text:
7. A Chinook salmon can jump out of water with a speed v0 and an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal. What is the speed of the fish when it is at the maximum height?
A. \(v_0\).
B. \(v_0 \cos \theta\).
C. \(v_0 \sin \theta\).
D. 0.
datasource_item.generated_question_text:
Q7. A tennis ball is launched with speed \(u_0\) at an angle \(\phi\) above the horizontal (ignore air resistance). What is the speed of the ball when it is at the maximum height?
A. \(u_0\).
This is incorrect because the vertical component changes due to gravity, so the total speed generally decreases before the peak.
B. \(u_0\cos\phi\).
This is correct because at the top the vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal component remains \(u_0\cos\phi\), so the speed equals that value.
C. \(u_0\sin\phi\).
This is incorrect because \(u_0\sin\phi\) is the initial vertical component, which is not the speed at maximum height.
D. 0.
This is incorrect because only the vertical component becomes zero at the top, not the horizontal component.

D. None of the above is correct.

10. An object can escape a planet with radius R and mass M at an escape speed given by \(v = \sqrt{2GM/R}\), where \(G\) is the universal gravitational constant. Based on this expression for escape speed, which of the following statements is correct?

A. Doubling the planet’s mass doubles the escape speed.
This is incorrect because \(v\) scales with \(\sqrt{M}\), so doubling M multiplies \(v\) by \(\sqrt{2}\), not 2.
B. For the same planet, a heavier spacecraft needs a larger escape speed.
This is incorrect because the formula shows escape speed depends on M and R of the planet, not the spacecraft’s mass.
C. For planets with the same mass, a larger radius gives a larger escape speed.
This is incorrect because increasing R decreases M/R, which reduces v.
D. A planet with four times the mass and half the radius has a higher escape speed.
This is correct because \(v \propto \sqrt{M/R}\), so replacing \(M \to 4M\) and \(R \to R/2\) increases M/R by a factor of 8, increasing v.

B. The magnitude of the acceleration is 1.6 m/s².
This is incorrect because 1.6 m/s² is a coefficient in position, not the (time-varying) acceleration.
C. The magnitude of the acceleration at t = 0 is 0 m/s².
This is incorrect because the constant term in a(t) is nonzero after taking two derivatives.

This is incorrect because it ignores that momentum is shared with the astronaut, greatly reducing the final speed.
D. 1.1 m/s.
This is incorrect because it overestimates the result by not accounting for the astronaut’s much larger mass compared with the tool.

This is correct because \(\Delta\vec{r} = (5.0\,\mathrm{m})\hat{\jmath}\) and \(W = \vec{F}\cdot\Delta\vec{r} = (6.00)(5.0) = 30.0\,\mathrm{J}\).

This is incorrect because it comes from using the force magnitude times displacement instead of the dot product component along the motion.

This is incorrect because it incorrectly uses the x-component of force even though there is no x-displacement.
D. 0 J.
This is incorrect because the force has a nonzero component along the direction of motion (\(\hat{\jmath}\)), so the dot product is not zero.
